objective.statement: See that one pitch can be written in the treble and the bass clef.
successCriteria: I know middle C is the first ledger line below the treble stave and above the bass stave.
I can find the same pitch in the other clef.
I know the pitch is the same even though the writing looks different.

explanation.text: The treble clef and the bass clef each cover a range of pitches, and the ranges meet near middle C. That means the same pitch can be written in either clef.

music.textAlternative: A treble stave with middle C on the first ledger line below.

explanation.caption: Middle C in the treble clef: on the first ledger line below the stave.

music.textAlternative: A bass stave with middle C on the first ledger line above.

explanation.caption: Middle C in the bass clef: on the first ledger line above the stave. It is the same pitch as the one before.

explanation.text: Neighbouring notes work the same way. D is in the space just below the treble stave, and in the space above the first ledger line in the bass clef. A is on the second ledger line below the treble stave, but the top line of the bass stave.
A note always keeps its pitch. Only its position on the page changes when the clef changes.
When a note sits near middle C, ask which clef you are in, then count from that clef's stave.

music.textAlternative: Five bass-clef notes climbing from the top line to the second ledger line above: A, B, C, D, E.

steps: A is the top line of the bass stave. B is the space just above it.
C is on the first ledger line above the bass stave: that is middle C.
D is the space above it and E is on the second ledger line. All of these pitches can also be written in the treble clef, below the stave.
demonstration.textAlternative: Bass-clef notes A, B, C, D and E climbing above the stave: the same pitches can be written below the treble stave.
